opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's a rare combination of things. Noam has this ability to pick problems that really matter, problems that are hard enough to be meaningful but where he has a real conviction that they're actually solvable. Poker was a great example. A lot of people thought no-limit hold'em was a long way off, and he just kept chipping away at it for years.

The other thing is his persistence. He doesn't get distracted by whatever's trendy. He'll stick with a direction when it isn't fashionable, and he's willing to keep iterating when things don't work the first, second, or tenth time. That kind of patience is underrated in research.

And he's very grounded. He cares about results that actually hold up: rigorous evaluations, real benchmarks, beating strong humans rather than just posting a nice number on a toy problem. That keeps his work honest.

Then there's search and planning. He's always believed that letting a model think at inference time, rather than just relying on the raw policy, gives you enormous gains. That insight carried from poker to Diplomacy and on to reasoning in language models, and he held onto it for a long time before it became the mainstream view.

On a personal level, he's generous with his time. When I was starting out, his work, and talking with him, shaped a lot of how I think about these problems. He's the kind of researcher who makes the people around him better.

fable-5.1.text:
Noam is just relentlessly clear about what matters. I worked with him on poker research back when I was quite young, and the thing that struck me immediately was that he doesn't get seduced by elegant ideas. He asks one question over and over: does this actually make the system better, and can I measure that? A lot of researchers fall in love with a method. Noam falls in love with the problem.

The second thing is patience. He spent years on imperfect-information games when most of the field thought it was a niche, and he kept pushing on search and planning at test time when everyone else was obsessed with scaling training alone. That bet looks obvious now with reasoning models, but it wasn't obvious then. He was willing to be unfashionable for a long time because he was convinced by the evidence, not by the crowd.

And he's a very good engineer, which people underrate. Pluribus didn't win because of one clever trick. It won because every piece was tuned, tested, and understood. He'd sit down and actually look at the hands the bot played and ask why it did something strange. That combination of taste, stubbornness, and willingness to do the unglamorous work is rare. Most people have one or two of those. He has all three.

astra-6.text: I think one of Noam’s biggest strengths is his ability to identify a really important problem and stay focused on it. He combines deep technical thinking with a willingness to pursue ideas that might take years to pay off. And he’s good at questioning assumptions—asking whether something is actually a limitation or simply the way people have been approaching the problem. That combination of judgment, patience, and technical depth is incredibly valuable in research.

sol-6.1.text: I think one of Noam’s biggest strengths is his ability to identify the question that really matters and then stay focused on it. There are lots of interesting problems you could work on, but he’s very good at asking, “If we solve this, does it actually change what’s possible?” And he combines that ambition with a willingness to get into the details and test whether the idea works. That’s a powerful combination.
